full_judgment:
15. The claim of title and possession to the suit land has two dimensions. The plain-tiffs claim title and possession followed by dispossession from the suit land, on the basis of auction purchase, boinama, dhakhalnama, sale deed and lease from the Government in pursuance of settlement case and kabuliayat. Conversely, defendant No.1 claims title and possession to the suit land on the basis of Salami receipt, rent receipts and oral gift from his father Tazem Ali Hawlader. The burden of proof as per Sections 101 and 102 of the Evidence Act, 1872 primarily rests upon the plaintiffs to prove their claims. Rules 1 and 2 of Order-XVIII of the Civil Procedure Code, 1908 also provides that the plaintiff has right to begin and shall produce his evidence in support of the issues which he is bound to prove. 

 16. On perusal of the documents on record, it appears that 12 decimals of land of Plot No.935 of SA Khatian No.789 under Amtalimouza belong to Abdus Sattar, Birendra Bijoy Das and others. The aforesaid land was auctioned on 30.06.1986 and plaintiff No. 3 purchased the same. On 14.02.1987, plaintiff No.3 by a registered deed of sale transferred six decimals of land of Plot No.935 to plain-tiff No. l. Plaintiff Nos.3 and 1 mutated their names. Bijendra Bijoy Das, father of plaintiff No.3 achieved pattan of 3 decimals of land of Plot No.921 and 7 decimals of land of Plot No.934 in total 10 decimals of land from khas khatian No.1 of the Government through Settlement Case No.2(Am) of 1985-86. A Kabuliyat deed was registered on 12.11.1986 after having salami of taka 1750 and a new khatian No. 1326 was created in the name of Birendra Bijoy Das. The plaintiffs exhibited original parcha of SA khatian No.1326, certified copy of Kabuliyat dated 12.1.1.1986, the boinama and dakhalnama of certificate case No. 827(Am) of 1980-81, DCR of payment of salami taka 1.750 dated 10.11.1986, certified copy of SA Khatian No.789 and certified copies of order sheet of Settlement Case No.2(Am)/ 85-86.In the instant suit, the plaintiffs have produced documentary evidence, most of which are public in nature, regarding their title to the suit land. They also produced documentary evidence dhakhalnama and rent receipts in support of their possession to the suit land before dispossession. Simultaneously, they produced oral evidence in support of their title and possession followed by dispossession from the suit land. It appears that Pw-1 consistently deposed in support of the plaint that they took possession of the suit land in accordance with certificate case, boinama, dakhalnama, sale deed, and kabuliyat but on 23'02/1990 corresponding to 11 Falgoon, 1396 B.E. Defendant No.1 dispossessed them from the suit lard by force. Pw-1 did not depose contrary to his statement during cross-examination. Pw-2 and Pw-3 duly corroborated the testimony of Pw-1 regarding the plaintiffs' title and possession (before dispossession) to the suit land. It appears that Pw-2 materially corroborated the testimony of Pw-1 to the effect that on 11 Falgoon, 1396 B.S. defendant No.1 dispossessed the plaintiffs from the suit land. Likewise, Pw-3 substantially corroborated the testimony of Pw-1 that during 1396 B.S. defendant no 1 dispossessed the plaintiffs from the suit land. It appears that the plaintiffs have primarily been able to prove their title and possession (before dispossession) to the suit land and they have discharged their initial burden of proof. Now it is the turn of defendant No.1 to discharge his onus of proof. In terms of Section 102 of the Evidence act, 1872, the initial onus to prove its claim is always on the plaintiff and if he discharges that onus and makes out a case which entitles him to a relief, the onus shifts to the defendant to prove these circumstances, if any, which would disentitle the plaintiff to the same [Bharat Alumnium Co.-V- Maharashtra Alumnium Co., 2009 DLT 489]. In a suit for possession based on title once the plaintiff has been able to create a high degree of probability so as to shift the onus on the defendant, it is for the defendant to discharge his onus and in the absence thereof, the burden of proof lying on the plaintiff shall be held to have been discharged so as to amount to proof of the plaintiffs title [R. V. E. Venkatachala Gounder -V- Arulmigu Viswesaraswaini and V. P. Temple, AIR 2003 SC 4548]. Let us have an overview of the defendant's case to see defendant No.1 has been able to discharge his onus of proof. 

 17. The disputed land is presently situated at Amtali Upazila of Borguna District which was formerly included in the subdivision of Patuakhali. Defendant No.1 in support of his title to the suit land produced an unregistered salami receipt dated 5 Baishakh, 1359. BS and Dakhila dated 15.08.1360 BS. The trial Court and the Appellate Court were of the view that at date of execution of the salami receipts on 5 Baishakh, 1359 BS corresponding to 18th April 1952 AD Zamindari system was not prevalent because of the coming into force of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act, 1950 (hereinafter referred to as the SAT Act) and, therefore, Zamindars had no right to give pattan of their land at that time. But the High Court Division took a different view on the point of coming into force of Part-V of the SAT Act stating that Part-V of this Act came into force in the Sub-Division of Patuakhali on 5th August, 1954 AD. The view taken by the High Court Division on the point of coming into force of Part-V of the SAT Act appears to be correct since Part-V of the SAT Act came into force in entire area of Patuakhali Sub-Division of the District of Bakcrganj with effect from the date of publication of the notification in the Dacca Gazette, vide Notification No.9918-LR., date 8th July 1954, published in the Decca Gazette, date 5th August, 1954, Part-I, p. 890 (SAT ACT DLR by Obaidul Huq Chowdhury, Fifth Edition-2015, page 242- 243].Hence, in the Subdivision of Patuakhali Zamindars had right to give pattan of their land by receiving salami before 5th August, 1954. But the question pertaining to this case is whether Naeb Shailendra Nath Saha executing the salami receipt on behalf of the Zamindars gave the same to the father of defendant No.1, Tazem Ali Hawlader and delivered possession of the suit land to him or not? The salami receipts and rent receipts were marked as exhibits with objection. Salami receipt and dakhila are private documents and those will not be admissible in evidence as genuine documents on the mere production of the same. The genuineness of the salami receipt has to be determined in the light of the facts and circumstances of the instant case. The Appellate Court held that the salami receipt/lease document is not genuine itself since it is rubbed and has cut marks and the back page of it is covered by white paper. This view of the Appellate Court regarding the title document of defendant No.1 seems to be based on proper appreciation of the documentary evidence on record in the light of the facts and circumstances of the instant case. In the case of Ajufannessa @ AjiBibi and others-Vs-Safar Miah and others, 30 D.L.R (AD) 41 it was held that "A private document can-not be taken notice of and marked as an Exhibit without any formal proof, unless the requirement of such proof is waived by the opposing party. The marking of the said document as an exhibit may, however, give rise to a belief that it bears the writing or signature of a person, as has been deposed to by the witness who proves the said document. The question as to whether the document is a genuine one or it represents the true state of affairs is a question of fact which is to be decided by the Court concerned in the light of the facts and circumstances of the case. There is no legal presumption which the Court is bound to make in respect of such a document. There is no such law as requires a Court to presume that a rent receipt purported to be granted by a landlord in favour of a certain person is genuine and what has been written in such a rent receipt are true. In this case, both of the courts of fact have decided the question of genuineness of the disputed rent receipts in the light of the facts and circumstances of the case and have also examined their various features with reference to the surrounding facts and came to the definite finding as to their spurious character. Such a finding is binding upon the High Court in a Second Appeal unless it could be shown that the said finding had been vitiated by an error of law or procedure which had affected the merits of the case." The ratio of this case was again reiterated in the case of Md. Jashimuddins Kanchan -Vs- Md. Ali Ashraf (42 DLR (AD) 289]. The High Court Division did not reverse this finding of the Appellate Court that the genuineness of the salami receipt is highly doubtful. Since the tide document of the father of defendant No.1 is highly doubtful, subsequent transfer of the same property to defendant No.1 by oral gift is also doubtful. Defendant No.1 claimed that during 1961 his house at the disputed land was destroyed by cyclone for which he repaired the same with his own expense. But he deposed,  “১৯৬১ সালে আমি ৬ষ্ঠ শ্রেণীতে পড়তাম। তখন আমার ব্যক্তিগত আয়ের উৎস ছিলনা।" This portion of the deposition of Dv-1 suggests that the claim of defendant No.1 regarding his possession of the suit property from 1960 onward is apparently baseless. It appears that father of defendant No.1 and thereafter, defendant No.1 did not take any time worthy step whatsoever for correction of the record of rights. The possession of the defendant No.1 in the suit land cannot be traced back to any valid title whereas the possession (before dispossession) of the plaintiffs in the suit land can be traced back to valid title which coupled with attending facts and circumstances reasonably gives rise to the presumption that the plaintiffs were dispossessed from the suit land by defendant No.1 by force. 

 19. Upon perusal of the Judgment of the High Court Division it appears that the High Court Division on erroneous belief decided the case keeping in view of section-9 of the Specific Relief Act, 1877. But the pleadings of the parties clearly indicate that this case is brought under section-8 of the Specific Relief Act, 1877 read with Article 142 of schedule-1 to the Limitation Act, 1908 and, therefore, the plaintiffs case file the suit for recovery of possession within 12 years from the date of dispossession. The finding by the High Court Division to the effect that the notice by the government to defendant No.1 to vacate possession cast a substantial doubt in believing the plaintiffs' case does not seem to be correct since possession of defendant No.1 can never be adverse to the government without defendant No. 1 is 60 years continuous adverse possession as per article 149 of schedule-1 of the Limitation Act, 1908 which is absent in the present case. 18. The trial Court as well as the Appellate Court arrived at concurrent finding that the plaintiffs have been able to prove their title and possession following by dispossession from the suit land. It appears that the findings of the trial court as well as the Appellate Court are based on the proper appreciation of evidence on record both oral and documentary. It is well settled position in law that under section 115 of the Code of Civil Procedure, the High Court cannot re-appreciate the evidence and cannot set aside the concurrent findings of the Courts below by taking a different view of the evidence. The High Court is empowered only to interfere with the findings of fact if the findings are per-verse or there has been a non-appreciation or non-consideration of the material evidence on record by the Courts below. Simply because another view of the evidence may be taken is no ground by the High Court to interfere in its revisional jurisdiction [Masjid Kacha Tank, Nahan-Vs-Tuffail Mohammed, AIR 1991 SC 455]. The civil cases are decided on the basis of preponderance of probability. Civil cases are decided on the basis of pre-ponderance of evidence while in a criminal case the entire burden lies on the prosecution and proof beyond reasonable doubt has to be given [Vishnu Dutt Sharma-V-Daya Sapra 13 SCC (2009) page 729]. In view of the facts, circumstances and proposition of law discussed above, we are of the view that the preponderance of probability regarding title and possession (before dispossession) of the plaintiffs to the suit land is clearly in favour of the plaintiffs and, therefore, the High Court Division made serious error of law in making the rule absolute which occasioned failure of justice.
